stories.take:
The Devils have acquired three-time Vezina Trophy winner Connor Hellebuyck from the Jets in a five-player trade, per The Hockey News and ESPN, ending a long standoff between the goalie and Winnipeg. The Athletic calls it a "long, messy saga" and says the deal makes New Jersey a contender.

The numbers show why the Devils wanted him. So far this season, NJD controls 58.6% of expected goals (a measure of shot quality) overall and 60% at five-on-five, yet sits at 6-4-0. The problem is in net: the team's goals saved above expected is -5.3, meaning its goalies have let in about five more goals than the shots should have produced. WPG has the opposite profile. Its goalies sit at +5.6 while the team holds only 46% of expected goals, so the Jets have been leaning on goaltending. Hellebuyck's departure leaves that propped-up record exposed.

For New Jersey, a goalie of his caliber could turn strong process into wins. Dawson Mercer is a case in point. He has no goals and four points in 10 games despite 2.18 expected goals of his own, a gap of -2.18. Better goaltending would help the whole team convert its edge, but Mercer's finishing is a separate fix.

stories.take:
Vincent Desharnais is out four to six weeks after an emergency appendectomy on Thursday, the Capitals announced, per ESPN and Daily Faceoff.

The numbers say Washington loses a steadier piece than his three assists suggest. So far this season, the Capitals have controlled 54.6 percent of the expected goals (the quality of chances created and allowed) at five-on-five while Desharnais is on the ice, and the team's share runs about six percentage points better with him than without him. He has played 19.41 minutes a game, a real workload for a defenseman with no goals. That fits a role built on suppressing chances rather than producing them, so don't expect his absence to dent the scoring much, but it can show up in the defensive end. Washington already sits at 48.2 percent of expected goals overall and is 5-4-0, propped up by goaltending that has saved 4.9 goals more than expected. A thinner blue line with that cushion is worth watching. The sample is only nine games, so treat the on-ice splits as early reads, not fixed levels.

items.title: Two players placed on NHL waivers for Oct. 23

stories.take:
Daily Faceoff reports that defensemen Daemon Hunt of the Wild and Jack St. Ivany of the Jets have been placed on NHL waivers for Oct. 23 and are available to be claimed.

Hunt's numbers explain why Minnesota is willing to let him go. In 11 games so far this season he has no points, averaging 14.14 minutes a night. At five-on-five, the Wild controlled just 41% of the expected goals (a measure of shot quality) with him on the ice, and the team's share was about 19 percentage points better when he sat. St. Ivany's sample is only four games so far this season, so it says little either way. Winnipeg held 47% of the expected goals with him on the ice, and the team did slightly better, by about 2 points, when he played. Neither has a goal this season, and neither has been creating much offense on his own: each projects at 0.18 expected goals per 60 minutes. For a team claiming one, that makes either player a depth defender, not a fix. Hunt's on-ice results are the weaker of the two.

items.title: Red Wings, not Larkin, should be vilified for trade request

stories.take:
Per Daily Faceoff, the Red Wings, not Dylan Larkin, should be the ones vilified over his trade request, the outlet pointing to Detroit's 10 straight seasons without a playoff appearance, the longest drought in the NHL.

This site's numbers say the current team is better than its start suggests. DET is 4-3-3 with 11 points through 10 games, but it has earned 51.3 percent of the expected goals so far this season, meaning it has created slightly more of the quality chances than it has allowed. At five-on-five that rises to 52 percent. The gap is finishing: DET sits 6.1 goals below what its chances should have produced, so the shooting is the weak point, not the process. The goaltending is covering for it, with 3.4 goals saved above expected, which measures how many more goals the goalies have stopped than an average goalie would on the same shots. The power play (0.92 expected goals per game) and penalty kill (0.84 allowed per game) are middling inputs. A team playing even-to-better and under-scoring can see its results improve, which matters for how the drought story reads.

Goals minus expected, the gap between goals scored and the quality of chances taken, is minus 3.4. The Devils are 6-4-0 with 12 points, so the record is holding up better than the finishing and the saves.

The skaters are doing their part. NJD owns 58.6% of the expected goals, a measure of chance quality, and 60% at five-on-five. That is a team creating the better chances most nights. Fix the goaltending and the results should move toward what the chances suggest, which is why a goalie addition matters here more than most.

The Athletic reports on the mental toll of injuries, with the Avalanche's Gabriel Landeskog and Golden Knights' Jack Eichel describing how time away from the game affected their sense of identity. Neither player is listed as out right now, but both have returned to look like themselves.

Landeskog has four goals and six points in 10 games so far this season, and COL has had 55.89% of the 5-on-5 expected goals (a measure of chance quality) with him on the ice. His own expected goals are 2.45, so his four goals are 1.55 above what his chances suggest, and some of that scoring may cool off. Eichel has 18 points in 11 games, and VGK's 5-on-5 expected goal share is 59.58% with him playing, 7.91 percentage points better than without him. His goals are 1.73 above expected, but the playmaking and territorial impact look real.

If either has to miss time, going by how the coach has used his players, T.J. Hughes is next in line for Landeskog's minutes, and Mark Stone for Eichel's, with Braeden Bowman the likeliest to move up on the power play.

That matters for an Edmonton team that is 7-1-1 but whose 5-on-5 share is only an even 50 percent so far this season, with goalies that have been about 2.6 goals worse than expected. Going by how the coach has used his players, since Ekholm has not yet missed a game, Jake Walman (14:17 a night) is next in line for his minutes. Expect Walman to take a bigger share of the ice time while Ekholm is out.

The timing stings because Gibson's year has been shaky. So far this season he has a .873 save percentage over six games and sits 1.7 goals below what an average goalie would have saved on the same shots (goals saved above expected). Last season he was 10.11 goals better than expected over 57 games, so this looks like a slow start more than a new baseline. Detroit has still been decent in front of him: the team is 3-3-3 with 49.7 percent of the expected goals (a measure of chance quality), and the team's goalies have saved 3.5 goals more than expected overall. The bigger issue is finishing, with the Wings 7.1 goals below expected scoring. If Gibson misses time, Detroit's even-strength play (51 percent of expected goals at five-on-five) is good enough to stay in games, but the goaltending cushion thins. Fantasy managers holding Gibson should check for updates before locking lineups.

The Sharks' share of expected goals is 6.06 percentage points better with him on the ice, though his own 5-on-5 share is 47.92%. He has two goals against an expected 1.25, so some of his production was running a bit hot, but he scored 9 goals in 28 games last season and has held a regular role.

Going by how the coach has used his players, not games already played without him, Alexander Wennberg (20:21 a night) is next in line for Chernyshov's minutes, with the second power-play unit the other opening.

The Penguins are 3-5-1 with 7 points through 9 games, but they hold 49.3% of the expected goals (a measure of chance quality, so roughly an even split with opponents). At 5-on-5 that climbs to 55%, a clear edge. Pittsburgh has also scored 3 fewer goals than its chances would predict so far this season, which points to finishing and bad puck luck more than a broken team. Goaltending sits right at expectation, with goals saved above expected at 0, so the goalie isn't the culprit either.

That matters because a nine-game sample is small, and the underlying play doesn't yet make the case for a teardown. If the finishing recovers, the standings could improve without a roster change. Dubas has reason to wait before deciding which way to go.
